content: A tattoo is a permanent design created by introducing ink into the layers of the skin, altering its pigmentation for aesthetic or other purposes. Tattoos on humans are a form of decorative body modification, while tattoos on animals are typically used for identification or branding purposes. The practice of tattooing has been observed globally across various cultures and time periods. The indigenous Ainu people of Japan traditionally adorned their faces with tattoos. Today, facial tattoos can also be seen among the Berbers of Tamazgha and the Maori of New Zealand. Tattooing was widespread among Polynesian communities and certain tribal groups in regions such as the Philippines, Borneo, the Mentawai Islands, Africa, North and South America, Mesoamerica, Europe, Japan, Cambodia, New Zealand, and China. Despite cultural taboos in some areas, tattooing remains a popular art form worldwide. The term tattoo originates from the Samoan word tatau, which means to mark or to strike twice, referencing traditional tattooing methods. The first syllable, ta, meaning hand, is repeated as an onomatopoeic representation of the repetitive action, while the final syllable, u, translates to color. In Polynesian tattooing, the instrument used to pierce the skin is called a hahau, with ha meaning to strike or pierce. The word tattoo was first recorded in English in Captain James Cook's diary during his 1769 voyage to the Marquesas Islands, where he described the Polynesian custom of marking the body. Sailors from this voyage later introduced the term and the concept of tattooing to Europe. In Japan, traditional tattoo designs are referred to as Horimono, and the hand-poked method is called Tebori. The term Irezumi simply means insertion of ink and can refer to tattoos created using Tebori, Western-style machines, or any other method involving ink insertion. Japanese individuals may use the word tattoo to describe non-Japanese styles. Enthusiasts often refer to tattoos as tats, ink, art, or work, and tattooists are commonly called artists. This terminology has gained acceptance, with mainstream art galleries showcasing both traditional and custom tattoo designs. Mass-produced copyrighted tattoo designs sold to artists are known as flash, a notable example of industrial design. Flash sheets are prominently displayed in many tattoo parlors to inspire customers and provide ready-made tattoo options. Tattooing has been practiced in Eurasia since at least the Neolithic era. Ötzi the Iceman, dating back to the fourth or fifth millennium BC, was discovered in the Alps with approximately 57 carbon tattoos consisting of simple dots and lines on his lower spine, behind his left knee, and on his right ankle. Other tattooed mummies from the late second millennium BC have been found in Pazyryk on the Ukok Plateau. In Japan, tattooing is believed to date back to the Paleolithic era, around ten thousand years ago. Various cultures have developed their own tattooing traditions, ranging from rubbing cuts with ashes to hand-pricking the skin to insert dyes. Tattoos are created by embedding colored materials beneath the skin's surface. The earliest tattoos may have been accidental, resulting from soot or ashes rubbed into a wound, leaving a permanent mark after healing. Tattoo styles vary widely, including native, religious, wildlife and nature, oriental, symbolic, old school, fantasy, and portrait designs. Tattoos have served numerous purposes throughout history, such as rites of passage, status and rank markers, symbols of religious and spiritual devotion, decorations for bravery, sexual lures, fertility marks, pledges of love, punishments, amulets, talismans, protection, and identifiers for outcasts, slaves, and convicts. The symbolism and impact of tattoos differ across cultures and can sometimes have unintended consequences. Tattoos can also express personal feelings about loved ones, such as parents or children. Today, people choose tattoos for cosmetic, sentimental, memorial, religious, magical, or group identification reasons, including affiliations with criminal gangs or law-abiding subcultures. Some Maori individuals still wear intricate facial moko, while in Laos, Cambodia, and Thailand, yantra tattoos are believed to offer protection against evil and bring good luck. Tattoos have also been used for identification purposes, both voluntarily and forcibly. The most infamous example is the Nazi identification system for Jews during the Holocaust. However, tattoos can also serve positive identification purposes. For instance, Maori chiefs historically used their moko as signatures on documents. Forensic pathologists sometimes use tattoos to identify burned, decomposed, or mutilated bodies, as tattoo pigment is embedded deeply enough in the skin to survive severe burns. Many military personnel today have their identification tags tattooed on their ribs, known as meat tags. Animals are also tattooed for identification, such as pets, show animals, thoroughbred horses, and livestock. These tattoos are often performed by veterinarians, with the animals anesthetized during the process. Branding, a similar practice, does not involve ink or dye and is often performed without anesthesia. Cosmetic tattooing includes permanent makeup, such as enhancing eyebrows, lips, and eyes, or camouflaging skin discolorations. Medical tattoos are used to ensure proper instrument placement for repeated radiotherapy applications or to reconstruct the areola in breast reconstruction. Tattoos can also convey medical information about the wearer. Tattooing has experienced a resurgence in popularity, particularly in North America, Japan, and Europe. The growth of tattoo culture has attracted new artists with technical and fine art training, leading to improved tattoo quality. Advances in pigments and equipment have further enhanced the art form. Tattoos have become prominent in pop culture, inspiring television shows like Miami Ink and LA Ink. The decoration of blues singer Janis Joplin with tattoos by artist Lyle Tuttle marked a seminal moment in the acceptance of tattoos as art. Tattoos are also significant in the culture of the Russian Mafia and have seen a revival in traditional cultures as a nod to cultural heritage. Tattooing involves inserting pigment into the dermis, the connective tissue layer beneath the epidermis. The pigment is initially dispersed throughout the damaged skin layers, activating the immune system's phagocytes to engulf the particles. As healing progresses, the damaged epidermis flakes away, and granulation tissue forms in the dermis, trapping the pigment within fibroblasts. Over time, the pigment may migrate deeper into the dermis, causing old tattoos to lose detail. Traditional tattooing methods include cutting designs into the skin and rubbing the wounds with ink or ashes, as well as hand-tapping ink into the skin using sharpened sticks or animal bones. Modern tattooing primarily uses electric machines that rapidly insert ink into the skin with needles. These machines are sanitary, with single-use needles and disposable supplies. Proper hygiene and sterilization are essential in tattoo studios to prevent cross-contamination and infection. Tattoo aftercare varies, with recommendations including keeping the tattoo clean, avoiding prolonged sun exposure, and refraining from removing scabs. Specific products may be used to aid healing, and commercial aftercare products are now available. Tattoos can be removed, though complete removal may not always be possible. Laser removal is the most common method, breaking down the ink for absorption by the body. However, this process can be expensive, painful, and may result in scarring. Some individuals opt for cover-up tattoos to conceal unwanted designs. The tattoo industry has seen record-breaking achievements, such as the most tattoos completed in 24 hours. Tattooing continues to evolve as an art form, with advancements in techniques, equipment, and cultural acceptance.
